extracted.subtask_description: Editorial and reporting guidance about how newspapers should handle news, secrecy, and censorship in wartime — balancing national security and public information. Covers duties of the press, voluntary censorship codes, government-press cooperation, and regional/newsgathering practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to a voluntary code of censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers gave an impressive demonstration of their adherence to the voluntary code of censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntary suppression of certain wartime information is appropriate when in the country's best interest; many papers kept secrets voluntarily because it served national security. However, this adherence should not become a blank check for excessive secrecy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not publish information that endangers presidential or public safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers should not do anything that might endanger the safety of the President.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within the necessary limits of protection, the press should avoid reporting details (e.g., movements, itinerary) that could compromise safety. At the same time, such protective measures should be narrowly applied so as not to unduly restrict other legitimate reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit censorship to what is strictly necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: A censorship which permits the people of this nation to live in doubt that they are being fully informed on everything that properly can be printed, defeats its own purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suppress only information whose publication would harm national security; excessive suppression undermines public confidence and the purpose of wartime censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government obligation to explain reasons for censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: It would seem to be the Government's obligation to make clear to the public in each important instance the reasons which impel it to ask purveyors of news to put the fresh product into cold storage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asking the press to withhold news, authorities should, where possible, explain the rationale to preserve trust and reduce speculation; explanations need not reveal sensitive details but should justify the restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow greater freedom of the press when safety permits
rubrics_metrics.description: Yet, within such limit, room may exist for somewhat greater freedom than was permitted during the past two weeks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even during wartime, if publication does not materially risk security, the press should exercise its freedoms; officials and editors should assess and expand permissible reporting where safe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid arbitrary or capricious restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Times did not and does not agree with such arbitrary restrictions. This lack of agreement applies in many other respects to phases of wartime censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrictions should be consistent, reasonably justified, and not imposed as blunt, arbitrary measures that infringe press independence without clear security benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh suppression's effect on rumor and public confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Press and radio, pledged to silence, were unable to combat such rumors... the mere fact that it was made now will leave an aftermath of speculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and officials must consider that withholding news can create vacuum-filling rumors and speculation; when suppression will likely cause misinformation, that risk must be considered in deciding to withhold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose non-sensitive facts when possible to maintain trust
rubrics_metrics.description: There would have been no harm in announcing beforehand that Mr. Roosevelt would be absent for a time from Washington.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid appearance of secrecy and regain public trust, disclose benign facts (e.g., presidential absence) when they do not compromise safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve a free and independent press against 'news dictatorship'
rubrics_metrics.description: After his brief taste of news dictatorship he returned to Washington impatient with the free news... The Presidential tour ... exercised absolute control of all sources of news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentration of control over information sources (by government or executive) is harmful; the press must retain independence and capacity for free comment even while cooperating on security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government should cooperate with the press to 'sandpaper' friction
rubrics_metrics.description: The Government has made some effort to sandpaper the roughest places by enlisting the cooperation of advisers who understand what readers expect; but smoothness has not been fully attained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active liaison and explanation between government advisers and news organizations can reduce harmful friction; both sides should work to clarify what can and cannot be published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain categories of wartime news require official authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the wartime censorship code, the progress of conversion of the industrial machine for military purposes, new plants, the output of planes, guns and ships—all these require official authority for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting on industrial production, military movements, and similar sensitive categories should follow established censorship/code approval processes; editors must get clearance where required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use background briefings to aid judgment without violating security
rubrics_metrics.description: Small groups of reporters ... are taken regularly into the confidence of many high officials ... They are told as a matter of 'background information,' to aid them in judging developments and events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officials may provide off-the-record/background information to selected reporters so the press can contextualize events; reporters should use such material responsibly and not disclose sensitive details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance privileged access with obligation to uphold the war effort
rubrics_metrics.description: The American press balances its unique privileged position with a sense of obligation—to uphold the war effort and general confidence in great agencies of public intelligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With special access comes responsibility: the press should weigh public-interest reporting against potential harm to the war effort and act in a way that sustains public confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain regional/newsgathering structures to serve local readership
rubrics_metrics.description: The A.P. long ago set up a special regional staff—A.P. men and women drawn from the various States to keep an eye out for news of interest to their home localities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News organizations should retain or create regional correspondents to identify and report locally relevant stories, ensuring readers receive information that matters to their communities even during global conflicts.
